result.markdown: --- title: "Session 2 — Neighbours and Spatial Weights" subtitle: "Contiguity · k-nearest · weights · the spatial lag · sensitivity · Lab 2" author: "Community Medicine Workshop" format: revealjs: theme: serif css: [../assets/slide_deck.css, assets/workshop.css, assets/quiz.css] include-after-body: assets/quiz-include.html embed-resources: true slide-number: true navigation-mode: linear code-copy: true center: false transition: fade width: 1280 height: 720 fig-align: center html-math-method: plain execute: echo: true warning: false message: false fig-width: 9 fig-height: 4.6 fig-dpi: 100 --- ## Where we are ::: {.incremental} - Session 1: spatial data, CRS, joins, honest maps - Every spatial test asks: **are neighbouring areas more alike than chance?** - First we must **define "neighbour"**. That definition is the **spatial weights matrix**, the most influential choice in the analysis - By the end you can: - build **queen, rook, k-nearest** and **distance** neighbours - turn them into **row-standardised weights** - compute and read a **spatial lag** - check how sensitive a result is to the choice ::: # Topic 1 — Who is a neighbour? {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Contiguity: share a boundary ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} - **Rook:** share an **edge** - **Queen:** share an edge **or a corner** (the usual default) - Needs polygons; areas of similar size behave best - Watch for **islands**: areas with no neighbour ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nb_q <- poly2nb(blocks, queen = TRUE, snap = 1e-4) nb_r <- poly2nb(blocks, queen = FALSE, snap = 1e-4) c(queen_links = sum(card(nb_q)), rook_links = sum(card(nb_r))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` queen_links rook_links 414 414 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(nb_q) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Neighbour list object: Number of regions: 79 Number of nonzero links: 414 Percentage nonzero weights: 6.633552 Average number of links: 5.240506 Link number distribution: 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 1 7 13 20 28 9 1 1 least connected region: 3 with 2 links 1 most connected region: 24 with 8 links ``` ::: ::: ## Seeing the links ::: {.cell output-location='slide'} ```{.r .cell-code} cen <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(blocks)) plot(st_geometry(blocks), border = "grey70", main = "Queen contiguity") plot(nb_q, cen, add = TRUE, col = "red", pch = 19, cex = 0.4) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](s2_neighbours_weights_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=900} ::: ::: ::: {.key} Check three things in `summary()`: the **average number of neighbours** (about 5 here), the **least and most connected** blocks, and any **isolates** (they break most tests unless `zero.policy = TRUE`). ::: ## Distance and k-nearest neighbours ::: {.cell output-location='slide'} ```{.r .cell-code} knn5 <- knn2nb(knearneigh(cen, k = 5)) d <- unlist(nbdists(knn2nb(knearneigh(cen, k = 1)), cen)) nb_d <- dnearneigh(cen, 0, max(d)) par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) plot(st_geometry(blocks), border = "grey80", main = "5 nearest neighbours"); plot(knn5, cen, add = TRUE, col = "blue", pch = 19, cex = 0.3) plot(st_geometry(blocks), border = "grey80", main = "Distance band"); plot(nb_d, cen, add = TRUE, col = "darkgreen", pch = 19, cex = 0.3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](s2_neighbours_weights_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=1100} ::: ::: | Definition | Neighbours per area | Good for | Watch out for | |---|---|---|---| | Queen / rook | varies | polygons of similar size | islands; large areas have many neighbours | | k nearest | exactly k | unequal areas, points | links across a gap that are not real | | Distance band | varies | points, a travel-distance idea | too short: isolates; too long: everyone linked | # Topic 2 — From neighbours to weights {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## A neighbour list says who; weights say how much | Style | Meaning | |---|---| | `"B"` binary | 1 for every neighbour | | `"W"` **row-standardised** | each area's weights sum to 1; the usual choice | | `"S"` | variance-stabilising | ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lw <- nb2listw(nb_q, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE) lw$weights[[1]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.25 0.25 0.25 0.25 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} sum(lw$weights[[1]]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.key} With `"W"`, area *i* gives each of its *k* neighbours weight 1/*k*. An area with 2 neighbours weights each by 0.5; one with 8 by 0.125. ::: ## The spatial lag ::: {.eq} lag(x)~i~ = Σ~j~ w~ij~ x~j~ = **the average of i's neighbours** ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} blocks$lag_rate <- lag.listw(lw, blocks$dengue_per_100k, zero.policy = TRUE) c(lag_from_function = blocks$lag_rate[1], mean_of_neighbours = mean(blocks$dengue_per_100k[nb_q[[1]]])) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` lag_from_function mean_of_neighbours 27.825 27.825 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell output-location='slide'} ```{.r .cell-code} p1 <- ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = dengue_per_100k)) + scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", direction = -1, name = NULL) + labs(title = "Rate") p2 <- ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = lag_rate)) + scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", direction = -1, name = NULL) + labs(title = "Spatial lag (neighbours' average)") p1 + p2 ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](s2_neighbours_weights_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=1100} ::: ::: The lag is **smoother** than the original. Moran's I (Session 3) is essentially the slope of the lag on the value. # Topic 3 — Does the choice matter? {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Sensitivity ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} w_list <- list(queen = nb2listw(nb_q, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE), rook = nb2listw(nb_r, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE), knn5 = nb2listw(knn5, style = "W"), distance = nb2listw(nb_d, style = "W")) map_dfr(w_list, \(w) { m <- moran.test(blocks$dengue_per_100k, w, zero.policy = TRUE); tibble(I = round(unname(m$estimate[1]), 3), p = signif(m$p.value, 2)) }, .id = "weights") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 3 weights I p 1 queen 0.499 5 e-14 2 rook 0.499 5 e-14 3 knn5 0.511 1.80e-15 4 distance 0.543 1 e- 9 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - Here the pattern is strong, so the conclusion barely moves - With a **weak** pattern the answer can change with the weights - **Justify** the choice with the biology: how far does a mosquito, a patient or an exposure travel? - **Report** the weights and check sensitivity ::: ## Common mistakes ::: {.bad} - Using the default without saying which one - Ignoring isolates (silently dropping areas) or areas with 15 neighbours - Using contiguity for **points** (they have no boundaries) - Computing distances in **degrees** instead of a projected CRS ::: ## 🔧 Switch to R — Lab 2 {.lab-slide background-color="#1565c0"} ::: {.lab-box} **File:** `gis-workshop/labs/lab2_weights.R` - `poly2nb()` queen vs rook · `summary()` of a neighbour list - `knearneigh()` · `nb2listw()` · row sums - `lag.listw()` and a check by hand · Moran's I under four weights ::: **Time:** 30 minutes · answer the Q questions in the comments ## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s2q1" data-type="mcq" data-hash="eyk5wx.mugnt2" data-show="MSwgd2hhdGV2ZXIgdGhlIG51bWJlciBvZiBuZWlnaGJvdXJz" data-explain="Um93LXN0YW5kYXJkaXNhdGlvbiBkaXZpZGVzIGVhY2ggbmVpZ2hib3VyJ3Mgd2VpZ2h0IGJ5 IHRoZSBhcmVhJ3MgbmVpZ2hib3VyIGNvdW50LCBzbyBldmVyeSByb3cgc3VtcyB0byAxLiBU aGF0IG1ha2VzIHRoZSBsYWcgYSB3ZWlnaHRlZCBhdmVyYWdlLg=="} In row-standardised weights, what do the weights of one area add up to? - The number of neighbours of that area - 0, because the weights cancel out - 1, whatever the number of neighbours - The area's value divided by its population ::: ## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s2q2" data-type="mcq" data-hash="eykj5l.muh2ae" data-show="VGhlIG1lYW4gb2YgaXRzIDQgbmVpZ2hib3VycycgdmFsdWVz" data-explain="V2l0aCB3ZWlnaHRzIG9mIDEvNCBlYWNoLCB0aGUgbGFnIGlzIHRoZSBwbGFpbiBhdmVyYWdl IG9mIHRoZSBuZWlnaGJvdXJzJyB2YWx1ZXMu"} An area has 4 neighbours and row-standardised weights. What is its spatial lag? - The sum of its 4 neighbours' values - The mean of its 4 neighbours' values - Its own value minus the district mean - The value of its single nearest neighbour ::: ## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s2q3" data-type="mcq" data-hash="eykweb.muhgrs" data-show="UG9pbnRzIGhhdmUgbm8gYm91bmRhcmllcyB0byBzaGFyZSwgc28gY29udGlndWl0eSBkb2Vz IG5vdCBleGlzdA==" data-explain="Q29udGlndWl0eSBpcyBkZWZpbmVkIGJ5IHNoYXJlZCBwb2x5Z29uIGJvdW5kYXJpZXMuIEZv ciBwb2ludHMsIHVzZSBrLW5lYXJlc3Qgb3IgZGlzdGFuY2UtYmFzZWQgbmVpZ2hib3Vycy4="} Why are queen contiguity neighbours a poor choice for point data such as patient homes? - Points tend to have more than ten neighbours each - Queen contiguity needs the data in degrees, not in metres - Points have no boundaries to share, so contiguity does not exist - Contiguity can only be calculated for blocks with no missing data ::: ## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s2q4" data-type="mcq" data-hash="eyl9n1.muhv96" data-show="Q2hlY2sgaXQgaXMgcmVhbCwgdGhlbiBsaW5rIGl0IHNlbnNpYmx5IG9yIHVzZSB6ZXJvLnBv bGljeQ==" data-explain="SXNvbGF0ZXMgaGF2ZSBubyBuZWlnaGJvdXJzLCBzbyB0aGUgbGFnIGlzIHVuZGVmaW5lZC4g TG9vayBhdCB0aGUgbWFwLCBkZWNpZGUgYSBqdXN0aWZpZWQgbGluayAoZm9yIGV4YW1wbGUg ay1uZWFyZXN0KSBvciBhbmFseXNlIHdpdGggemVyby5wb2xpY3kgYW5kIHNheSBzby4="} summary(nb) reports one region with no neighbours (an island). What is the safest response? - Delete the region quietly so that the test runs without a warning - Give it the average value of the whole district to fill the gap - Ignore it, since one single area will not change the results - Check it is real, then link it sensibly or use zero.policy ::: ## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s2q5" data-type="mcq" data-hash="eylmvn.mui9qg" data-show="SXQgZGVwZW5kcyBvbiB0aGUgd2VpZ2h0cywgc28ganVzdGlmeSB0aGUgY2hvaWNlIGFuZCBy ZXBvcnQgc2Vuc2l0aXZpdHk=" data-explain="RGlmZmVyZW50IG5laWdoYm91ciBkZWZpbml0aW9ucyBjYW4gZ2l2ZSBkaWZmZXJlbnQgYW5z d2VycyB3aGVuIHRoZSBwYXR0ZXJuIGlzIHNjYWxlIGRlcGVuZGVudC4gUmVwb3J0IHdoaWNo IHdlaWdodHMgeW91IHVzZWQsIHdoeSwgYW5kIHdoYXQgaGFwcGVucyB3aXRoIG90aGVycy4="} Moran's I is 0.48 with queen weights and 0.12 with a distance band of 3 km. What is the best conclusion? - It depends on the weights, so justify the choice and report sensitivity - Queen weights are the standard choice, so the 3 km result can simply be ignored - The two values should be averaged to give the true value of Moran's I - The analysis has failed, so the test should be dropped from the report ::: ## Score and take-home **Your score: ** ::: {.incremental} - Weights turn 'near' into numbers; **choose them deliberately** - **Row-standardised** weights make the lag the **average of neighbours** - Check **isolates** and areas with very many neighbours - **Report** the weights and test sensitivity ::: **Next:** Session 3: global spatial autocorrelation

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
